tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — FOLLOW THE ENTIRE SIDE-OATS AXIS
tiles.details:
Flora field cue (Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, p. 1248) — Follow one long flowering axis and count its short side branches. The Flora gives usually 25–80.

Trace one attached flowering culm from the base of its panicle to the tip. Flora of North America reports usually 30–80 short reflexed branches (occasionally as few as 12), mostly 10–30 mm long, each usually bearing 2–7 spikelets. Orange/red dangling ANTHERS and pale feathery STIGMAS mark flowering, not seed awns. Use panels showing a whole flowering axis; color alone cannot prove species.
tiles.short: One long 13–30 cm flowering axis carries many short, drooping, mostly one-sided branches; each short branch is NOT one spikelet.
tiles.status: REAL HEAD ARCHITECTURE — BRANCH COUNT NOT CALIBRATED FROM IMAGES

tiles.heading: 02 · PERENNIAL BASE, COLLAR AND TRUE LIGULE
tiles.details: The species may be cespitose OR develop rhizomes; do not require every plant to be a solitary tuft. At the blade–sheath junction, separate the actual thin ligule membrane from neighboring collar hairs. FNA describes a 0.3–0.5 mm ciliate membrane, blades generally 2.5–7 mm wide and papillose-based hairs near the blade base. Existing whole-plant and leaf views do not resolve a measured ligule.
tiles.short: Perennial bunching or short-rhizomatous growth; true ciliate membranous ligule only about 0.3–0.5 mm.
tiles.status: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — OPENED LIGULE AND ROOTED SAME-PLANT BASE

tiles.heading: 03 · SHORT LATERAL BRANCHES AND SPIKELETS
tiles.details:
Flora field cue (Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, p. 1247) — Count spikelets on a single short branch. The Flora key groups this grass with Texas Grama as having usually 3–7 per branch. The number of branches on the entire head separates them.

A whole seedhead contains many lateral branches. Mature branches break off at their BASE, sometimes leaving a bare-looking main axis. Photograph an attached complete mature branch at 1-mm scale and count the actual spikelets before separating any glumes. External flowering photos establish architecture but not calibrated branch length or hidden spikelet structures.
tiles.short: Short deciduous branches usually 10–30 mm; usually 2–7 spikelets per branch, not 2–7 branches per head.
tiles.status: FIELD ARCHITECTURE SUPPORTED — NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO SCALED ATTACHED BRANCH

tiles.heading: 04 · GLUMES, FERTILE LEMMA AND SHORT AWNS
tiles.details:
On one source-authenticated mature spikelet, isolate the TWO outer glumes, then the basal bisexual fertile floret. FNA gives lower/upper glume lengths of 2.5–6/5.5–8 mm; glumes are generally awnless. The basal fertile lemma is 3–6.5 mm and 3-veined; veins may end in short mucros or awns up to about 6 mm. Do not label dangling flower anthers as lemma awns, or claim glume/lemma measurements from distant head photographs.

Photo still needed: one opened spikelet with both glumes and the fertile lemma separated beside a millimeter scale.
tiles.short: Lower glume 2.5–6 mm; upper glume 5.5–8 mm; fertile lemma 3–6.5 mm, three-veined.
tiles.status: PUBLISHED MEASUREMENTS — NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO DISSECTED GLUMES AND LEMMA

tiles.heading: 05 · UPPER STERILE FLORET AND CENTRAL TEXAS LOOK-ALIKES
tiles.details: FNA describes distal reduced florets about 0.4–3.5 mm; a reduced sterile lemma can carry three unequally developed awns, with the central awn about 1.5–7 mm. Blue grama has a few longer terminal eyebrow combs; hairy grama may show a conspicuous naked rachis extension; Texas grama has clustered short fuzzy terminal branches; red grama has much smaller narrow appressed branches. Do not call a one-sided branch diagnostic without seeing the entire axis and reproductive units.
tiles.short: One basal fertile floret plus 1–2 reduced sterile florets; inspect their awns separately from the fertile lemma.
tiles.status: LOOK-ALIKE LESSON — NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO FERTILE VS STERILE FLORET DISSECTION

tiles.heading: 06 · PUBLIC-READY GATE — RIGHTS AND PIXEL-ACCURATE ARROWS
tiles.details: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO (Grass Photo-Finish): same-plant rooted base and whole panicle; 0.3–0.5 mm true ligule at 10–20×; attached 10–30 mm mature side branch with 1-mm ruler; lower and upper glumes and 3–6.5 mm fertile lemma separated; reduced sterile lemma and its awns at scale. NEEDS_SITE_QA (Public Learner Readiness): verify public rights for each displayed panel, especially preserve UNKNOWN RIGHTS/public_reuse=no original image exclusion; check NC/SA conditions, existing arrows only on resolved pixels, attribution, and mobile learner rendering. No photo, arrow, license or website release is claimed here.
tiles.short: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS: excellent habit and flowering views, but no measured ligule or mature floret dissection.

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: FIRST trace the entire long CENTRAL SEEDHEAD AXIS: many short, oatlike lateral racemes hang along much of its length, often from one side. At bloom each raceme may carry vivid orange-red protruding anthers. Don't mistake ONE raceme for the whole seedhead. Confirm full flowering architecture before a species call.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: Perennial warm-season bunchgrass; culms erect to ascending from a tufted base.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: Mostly basal to lower-culm blades, narrow and flat to folded; margins and surfaces can feel rough.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: An elongated central axis bearing many short lateral racemes; the racemes characteristically hang or project from mostly one side.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Numerous short pendent RACEMES regularly spaced down a LONG flowering axis favor sideoats; blue grama has just a few longer terminal eyebrows, Texas grama several short dense fuzzy terminal branches, red grama tiny appressed units. Tumblegrass (Muhlenbergia paniculata) has much longer stiff divergent one-sided racemes rather than many short oats.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

panels.label: 3 · FLOWERING — orange anthers vs feathery stigmas · PROVISIONAL REVIEW
panels.caption: Bright orange tubes hanging down are pollen-bearing ANTHERS; fuzzy white delicate plumes projecting sideways are receptive STIGMAS. Both are reproductive parts and neither is an awn. No fertile-lemma length is measured here.
panels.creator: Erutuon
panels.modifications: Unmodified Commons-hosted photo, no annotations baked into source. Source JPEG unchanged by 2026-10-26 verification.
panels.annotation_note: Hays Botany displays overlaid numbered anatomy pointers; the source JPEG itself is unchanged.

panels.label: 4 · MATURING AXIS — one-sided short branches · PROVISIONAL REVIEW
panels.caption: The nearly continuous central flowering axis runs vertically through this photograph, carrying multiple small one-sided pendant RACEMES. The arrow onto one drooping lateral unit marks the whole little raceme with several spikelets, NOT a single spikelet. This mature head is connected to a flowering stem outside frame; it does not show the root crown or the true ligule.

intro: FIRST trace the entire long CENTRAL SEEDHEAD AXIS: many short, oatlike lateral racemes hang along much of its length, often from one side. At bloom each raceme may carry vivid orange-red protruding anthers. Don't mistake ONE raceme for the whole seedhead. Confirm full flowering architecture before a species call.
memory_rule: WHOLE AXIS → SHORT SIDE RACEMES → INDIVIDUAL SPIKELETS. Orange anthers and feathery stigmas are flowers, not bristles.
safety_note: Seven JPEGs physically found in GitHub, but images/04-inflorescence-architecture.jpg has UNVERIFIED LICENSE: keep it off the public gallery. Only anatomically visible gross features have existing arrows. Root/collar/spikelet dissections are still not complete.
field_rule: Numerous short pendent RACEMES regularly spaced down a LONG flowering axis favor sideoats; blue grama has just a few longer terminal eyebrows, Texas grama several short dense fuzzy terminal branches, red grama tiny appressed units. Tumblegrass (Muhlenbergia paniculata) has much longer stiff divergent one-sided racemes rather than many short oats.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.

morphology.habit: Perennial warm-season bunchgrass; culms erect to ascending from a tufted base.
morphology.leaves: Mostly basal to lower-culm blades, narrow and flat to folded; margins and surfaces can feel rough.
morphology.inflorescence: An elongated central axis bearing many short lateral racemes; the racemes characteristically hang or project from mostly one side.
morphology.spikelets: Several spikelets are packed along each short raceme; racemes detach as units when mature.
morphology.floral_detail: Reddish to orange anthers are often conspicuous during flowering.

eco_habitat: Prairies, open grasslands, roadsides, rocky calcareous sites, and managed native plantings across Central Texas.
